Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 111, verses 1–5:

﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.﴾ The meaning of "tabbat" is "khasirat" (lost, ruined), and al-tabab is al-khusran (loss, ruin). Abu Lahab is 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, and he was the paternal uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was among the most hostile of people toward him. If it is said: Why did Allah mention him by his kunya (teknonym) rather than his name? The answer is in three respects. First: his kunya was more dominant over him than his name, like Abu Bakr and others. It is said that he was given the kunya Abu Lahab because his face was aflame (talahhub) with beauty. Second: since his name was 'Abd al-'Uzza, He turned away from it to the kunya. Third: since he was among the people of the Fire and its flame, He gave him the kunya Abu Lahab, and to match this is His saying: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame.﴾

﴿His wealth did not avail him, nor what he earned.﴾ The "ma" may be negating or interrogative meaning negation. "Malahu" is his capital (ra's mal), and "ma kasab" is the profit; or "malahu" is what he inherited, and "ma kasab" is what he acquired for himself. It was said: "ma kasab" is all of his wealth. ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame.﴾ This is a definite decree that he will enter the Fire, and he died after that in disbelief. ﴿And his wife, the carrier of firewood.﴾ The name of his wife was Umm Jamil bint Harb ibn Umayyah, and she was the sister of Abu Sufyan. Regarding her description as "carrier of firewood" there are four opinions. The first: she would carry thorns and brushwood and throw them in the path of the Prophet (ﷺ) in order to harm him. The second: this is a metaphor for her walking about with slander (namimah); it is said: "So-and-so carries firewood between people," meaning he kindles the fire of enmity among them with tale-bearing. The third: it is a metaphor for her striving to cause harm to the Muslims; it is said: "So-and-so hatibs against so-and-so" when he intends to harm him. The fourth: it is a metaphor for her sins and the evil of her deeds. ﴿Around her neck is a rope of palm fiber.﴾ "Jid" is the neck, and "masad" is palm fiber; it was said: a twisted rope. Regarding what is meant by it there are three opinions. The first: it is a report of her carrying firewood in this world, according to the first opinion, and in that is a belittling of her and a display of the baseness of her condition. The second: it is her state in Hell, that it will be so, i.e., there will be a rope around her neck. The third: she had an expensive necklace, and she said, "I will spend it on enmity toward Muhammad," so He described her necklace as a rope of masad by way of omen and as a censure of her for her ostentation. The phrase "wa imratuhu" and what follows may admit of several grammatical analyses, and the pause (waqf) varies with them: that "imratuhu" and "hammalat al-hatab" is the predicate (khabar); or that "hammalat al-hatab" is an adjective (na't) and the predicate is "fi jiidiha hablun min masad"; or that "imratuhu" is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the pronoun in "yasla," and "hammalat al-hatab" is an adjective, or the predicate of an implied inchoative.
